q: Your diesel cranks at normal speed but will not fire. Which three things must it have to run?
a: Fuel, air and compression
o: Fuel, spark and compression
Spark, air and oil pressure
Fuel, spark and a full battery
why: A diesel has no spark: compression heats the air enough to ignite the injected fuel.

q: You trace the fuel line from the tank to the engine to find a leak. In what order do you meet the parts?
a: Water separator, lift pump, fine filter, injectors
o: Fine filter, lift pump, water separator, injectors
Lift pump, injectors, fine filter, water separator
Injectors, water separator, lift pump, fine filter
why: Fuel is cleaned twice on its way: coarse primary filter first, fine filter just before the injection pump.

q: During the morning check you look at the primary fuel filter bowl. What do you do?
a: Drain the water from the bowl until clean fuel runs
o: Leave it — it settles out by the next service
Top up the coolant — it is leaking into the bowl
Bleed the injectors — it is air in the fuel
why: Water is heavier than diesel and collects at the bottom of the separator; drain it before it reaches the engine.

fig.title: Primary filter / water separator
lines: Bottom 2 cm: a clear, separate layer
Fuel sits above it with a sharp line between

q: The engine has stopped twice in a week with a blocked filter. This is what you find. What is it?
a: Diesel bug growing where fuel meets water
o: Engine oil leaking into the fuel tank
Soot from the exhaust blown back in
Wax from the fuel in cold weather
why: Microbes live at the fuel–water layer and make sludge that blocks filters; keep tanks dry and treated.

fig.title: Fuel filter bowl
lines: Black-brown slimy sludge in the bowl
Boat little used, tank kept half empty

q: You ran the tank dry yesterday and have just put 60 litres in. The engine cranks strongly but will not start. Why?
a: Air in the fuel lines — bleed the system
o: Flat battery — switch to the house bank
Cold engine — hold the preheat longer
Blocked air filter — take it off and retry
why: Running dry pulls air into the fuel system; the injectors cannot spray air, so it must be bled.

fig.title: After running out of fuel
lines: No firing, no smoke at the exhaust

q: Bleeding the engine, you have opened the bleed screw on the fine filter. The lift pump has a hand lever. What next?
a: Pump the lever until fuel comes out bubble-free, then close
o: Crank the starter until diesel sprays out, then close
Close it at the first drop of diesel you see
Leave it open and start the engine to clear it
why: Bleed in the direction of the fuel flow and close each screw only when solid, bubble-free fuel runs.

q: You plan to motor through a calm day to the next fuel quay. How far can you go without touching your reserve?
a: 90 miles
o: 120 miles
60 miles
15 miles

lines: Calm sea, same revs all the way

q: Your next leg is 54 miles at 6 knots, at the same revs as before. How much fuel will you use?
a: 27 litres
o: 36 litres
18 litres
54 litres

fig.title: Fuel log
lines: Since then: 12 engine hours, cruising revs
Today the tank took 36 litres to brim

q: Fuel is getting low and the next fuel quay is 20 miles away into a short headsea. How do you stretch your range?
a: Ease back the revs a little
o: Run at full revs to get there sooner
Shift into neutral every half hour
Switch off the alternator to save power
why: Fuel use rises steeply near full throttle while speed barely does; a few hundred rpm less saves the most.

q: Motor-sailing hard on the wind, the engine stutters and stops. What is the most likely cause?
a: Low fuel sloshing away from the pickup
o: The engine overheated and cut out
The gearbox has seized under load
The raw-water impeller has broken
why: With a low tank and a big heel the pickup sucks air; level the boat, refuel and bleed.

lines: Oil alarm only after it stopped

q: You are about to start the engine at the berth. What is the right sequence?
a: Neutral, battery on, preheat, start, check exhaust water
o: Start, preheat, select neutral, then check the oil
Battery on, start in gear, then preheat if needed
Preheat, start, then open the raw-water seacock
why: Start in neutral so the boat cannot move, preheat a cold diesel, and confirm cooling water at once.

q: Early April in Croatia, you turn the key straight to start. What do you do differently?
a: Hold the preheat 10–15 seconds, then crank
o: Crank for a full minute without a break
Spray easy-start into the air intake
Open the throttle fully and keep cranking
why: Glow plugs heat the chambers so a cold diesel fires; ether with glow plugs can wreck the engine.

fig.title: Cold start
lines: Engine cranks well but does not catch
Puffs of white smoke at the exhaust

q: After three hours at cruising revs you reach the anchorage. How do you stop the engine?
a: Idle in neutral a few minutes, then stop
o: Stop it at once to save fuel
Rev it hard, then stop to clear soot
Turn the battery isolator off to stop it
why: A short idle lets heat even out before shutdown; never stop an engine with the isolator.

q: With the engine running, a crew member reaches for the battery isolator to turn it off and save power. What do you say?
a: Stop — it can blow the alternator diodes
o: Fine — the engine runs without the battery
Fine — the alternator then charges faster
Fine — but only at high revs
why: Opening the circuit while the alternator charges causes a voltage spike that destroys it.

q: You turn the key and hear one click, but the engine does not turn. What do you do?
a: Parallel the banks, then start the engine
o: Wait a day for the solar to charge it
Disconnect the house bank and keep trying
Turn the key to preheat for a full minute
why: The emergency parallel switch lets the house bank start the engine; separate the banks once it runs.

lines: Key turned: a click, no cranking

q: Motoring along the coast, you see this. What do you do?
a: Stop the engine at once and check the oil
o: Reduce revs and carry on to port
Top up the coolant and carry on
Ignore it — oil alarms are often false
why: Without oil pressure the bearings are destroyed within minutes; stop first, then investigate.

q: You turn the key to ON before starting. This is what you see and hear. What does it mean?
a: Normal — they go out once the engine runs
o: Low oil — top up before starting
Flat battery — switch to the house bank
Broken alternator — call the base
why: With the engine stopped there is no oil pressure and no charge, so both lights and the buzzer come on.

lines: Key at ON, engine not yet started

q: Ten minutes after leaving the marina you see this. What do you check first?
a: The alternator drive belt
o: The raw-water strainer
The engine oil level
The glow-plug relay
why: A charge light on with the engine running means the alternator is not charging; a slipping or broken belt is the usual cause.

q: Motoring out of Kos, you hear a squeal, then quiet. Soon after the panel looks like this. Most likely cause?
a: The belt has broken
o: The raw-water strainer is blocked
The engine oil is low
The propeller is fouled
why: One belt drives both the alternator and the coolant pump, so no charge plus rising heat points to it.

lines: Plenty of water at the exhaust

q: You follow the raw-water cooling circuit through the boat. In what order does the seawater go?
a: Seacock, strainer, impeller pump, heat exchanger, exhaust
o: Strainer, seacock, heat exchanger, impeller pump, exhaust
Seacock, impeller pump, exhaust, strainer, heat exchanger
Heat exchanger, seacock, strainer, exhaust, impeller pump
why: Seawater is filtered, pumped through the heat exchanger and then injected into the exhaust to cool it.

q: You have stopped the engine and let it cool. Where do you look first?
a: The raw-water strainer
o: The fuel filter
The engine oil level
The battery terminals
why: Floating weed or plastic is the commonest cause of lost cooling water; the strainer catches it.

fig.title: Overheat
lines: Motored through a bay full of floating weed
Temperature alarm, little water at exhaust

q: You take out the raw-water impeller. This is what you find. What do you do?
a: Find the missing pieces before fitting the new one
o: Fit the new one; the pieces wash out the exhaust
Refit the old one; four vanes are still enough
Fit the new one and run at high revs to clear it
why: Broken vanes travel on and block the heat exchanger inlet; recover every piece.

fig.title: Old impeller
lines: Two vanes broken off and missing

q: The coolant level is low on a freshwater-cooled engine. Where and how do you top it up?
a: Header tank, engine cold, with coolant mix
o: Raw-water strainer, engine running, with seawater
Header tank, engine hot, with seawater
Oil filler, engine cold, with fresh water
why: The closed circuit holds antifreeze coolant under pressure; open the cap only when cold.

q: The engine will not fire. Before you crank again, what do you do?
a: Close the raw-water seacock until it fires
o: Keep cranking — it will catch once warm
Open the strainer lid to let air out
Give it full throttle and crank a minute
why: Cranking without firing keeps pumping water into the waterlock until it floods the engine; reopen once it runs.

q: The temperature keeps rising. What is the most likely cause?
a: Low coolant on the freshwater side
o: Weed blocking the raw-water strainer
An impeller with missing vanes
A raw-water seacock half closed
why: Raw-water faults show as weak exhaust water; a strong flow points to the freshwater circuit.

q: Motoring into a headsea at cruising revs, what does this tell you?
a: The engine is overloaded or short of air
o: Water has got into the fuel
The engine is burning its own oil
Coolant is leaking into the cylinders
why: Black smoke is unburnt fuel: too much load (fouled hull or prop, headsea) or a blocked air intake.

fig.title: Exhaust
lines: Revs drop when you open the throttle
Water flow at the exhaust normal

q: After an hour at cruising revs you see this. What does it tell you?
a: Burning oil — report it to the base
o: Overloaded — ease back the throttle
Water in the fuel — drain the bowl
Warming up — it will clear soon
why: Blue smoke is oil burning in the cylinders: worn rings or valve seals, or an overfilled sump.

fig.title: Exhaust
lines: Oil on the dipstick lower than this morning

q: On a cool morning the engine starts with white smoke that clears within a minute. What do you do?
a: Nothing — normal for a cold diesel
o: Stop — the head gasket has failed
Stop — there is water in the fuel
Rev it hard to burn the smoke off
why: Some unburnt fuel and vapour are normal until the cylinders warm up.

fig.title: Start-up
lines: Air 10 °C, first start of the day
Good water flow at the exhaust

q: During the daily check, the oil on the dipstick looks like this. What do you do?
a: Do not start it — call the base
o: Run it to dry the oil out
Top up with fresh oil and go
Drain the fuel filter bowl
why: Milky oil means water in the engine (head gasket, cooler or siphoning exhaust); running it wrecks the bearings.

fig.title: Dipstick
lines: Level slightly above the max mark
Oil light brown and milky, like latte

q: You want an accurate reading of the engine oil level. When do you check it?
a: Engine stopped a while, boat level
o: Engine running at idle, boat level
Straight after stopping a long motor
Any time, even heeled under sail
why: Oil must drain back to the sump and lie level for the dipstick to read true.

q: During the daily check you press the alternator belt. What does this tell you?
a: Slack and wearing — get it tensioned
o: Normal — belts loosen when warm
Too tight — slacken it off a little
Normal — the dust is from the exhaust
why: A belt should deflect about 1 cm under thumb pressure; black dust is rubber worn off a slipping belt.

fig.title: Alternator belt
lines: Deflects about 3 cm under your thumb
Shiny sides, black dust around the pulleys

q: Coming into the berth you need to go from ahead to astern. How do you shift?
a: Throttle to idle, pause in neutral, then astern
o: Straight from ahead to astern at cruising revs
Shift at any revs once the boat is slow
Stop the engine, then select astern
why: Shifting at idle through neutral protects the gearbox and the clutch.

q: Motoring along the coast off Paros, you notice this. What is the most likely cause?
a: A line or net round the propeller
o: The fuel filter is partly blocked
The gearbox oil level is too low
The raw-water strainer is blocked
why: Vibration with lost speed at normal revs is a fouled prop; stop and check before it damages the shaft.

fig.title: Under power
lines: Speed 3 kn at your usual cruising revs
You crossed a line of fishing floats

q: In astern your stern walks to port. You must turn round in a narrow marina fairway. Which way do you turn?
a: To starboard — astern kicks the stern to port
o: To port — astern bursts kick the bow to port
Either way — prop walk only matters at speed
To port — the bow follows the prop walk
why: Short bursts ahead with full starboard helm and astern in between both rotate the boat clockwise.

fig.note: Narrow fairway · stern walks to port in astern

q: Reversing towards the quay with sternway on, you want the stern to go to port. Which way do you turn the wheel?
a: To port — astern, the stern follows the wheel
o: To starboard — astern, steering is reversed
Amidships — steer with prop walk only
To starboard — astern, the bow follows the wheel
why: With sternway on, the stern moves the way you turn the wheel.

q: Stopped in a tight marina, you want to swing the stern sideways without gaining much speed. What do you do?
a: Rudder hard over, a short burst ahead
o: Rudder hard over, a long gentle push astern
Rudder amidships, a short burst astern
Rudder hard over, coast in neutral
why: Prop wash over the rudder turns the boat before she gathers way.

q: Motoring slowly ahead, you turn to port. Which part of your boat swings towards the moored yacht?
a: The stern — it swings out opposite the turn
o: The bow — the boat pivots round the stern
Neither — the boat pivots round its middle
The bow — it always swings towards the wind
why: Going ahead a yacht pivots about a third from the bow, so the stern swings wide.

fig.note: Turning to port, moored yacht close to starboard

q: You approach the fuel quay at 4 knots, planning a hard burst astern at the last moment. What is the problem?
a: She carries way and the stern kicks sideways
o: None — astern stops a yacht in her own length
The engine always stalls when shifted astern
The rudder locks hard over when you go astern
why: A heavy yacht needs several lengths to stop, and prop walk swings the stern; come in slowly.

q: Your charter catamaran is stopped in the marina. You want to spin her to starboard on the spot. What do you do?
a: Port engine ahead, starboard engine astern
o: Starboard engine ahead, port engine astern
Both engines ahead, wheel hard to starboard
Port engine astern, starboard in neutral
why: Twin screws far apart give a turning couple: push one side forward and pull the other back.

fig.note: Catamaran, twin engines · turn to starboard

q: You check the stern gland of a traditional packed shaft. What do you do?
a: Nothing — a slow drip keeps it cool
o: Tighten it until it is fully dry
Close the cockpit drain seacock
Stop the engine and call the base
why: Packing needs a few drops a minute with the shaft turning to lubricate and cool it.

fig.title: Stern gland, engine in gear
lines: Packed gland on a turning shaft
Two or three drops a minute
No drips with the shaft stopped

q: This is your morning check on a saildrive boat. What do you do?
a: Seawater is in the leg — report it now
o: Normal condensation — top it up later
Coolant leak — top up the header tank
Diesel bug — drain the fuel filter bowl
why: Milky saildrive oil means the lower seals let seawater in; the leg can fail and must be inspected.

fig.title: Saildrive check
lines: Engine oil: clean, at the mark

q: At check-in you lift the floor over the saildrive. What do you do?
a: Report it — the hull seal may be leaking
o: Normal — the seal is meant to weep
Normal — it is rain from the cockpit
Sponge it dry and check again next week
why: The rubber diaphragm is the only seal round a big hole in the hull; any seawater there is serious.

fig.title: Saildrive well
lines: Seawater pooled on top of it

q: Holding the bow off the berth against a crosswind, you have run the bow thruster without a break. It now stops. Why?
a: It overheated and cut out — use short bursts
o: The engine is off — the thruster needs it in gear
The thruster's shear pin has broken
The thruster fuse is meant to blow each time
why: Thrusters are built for short bursts; a thermal cut-out stops them when they overheat.

q: Motor-sailing off Lefkada, this happens. What do you do?
a: Fit the emergency tiller and steer with it
o: Press Standby — the autopilot is slipping
Turn the wheel harder to free the jam
Call Mayday — the rudder has fallen off
why: A slack wheel means the cable or linkage has failed; the emergency tiller goes straight on the rudder stock.

fig.title: Steering
lines: Boat rounds up, no response to the wheel
No bang, no water coming in

q: You are on autopilot when a fishing boat appears ahead. You need to steer by hand at once. What do you do?
a: Press Standby, then take the wheel
o: Turn the wheel hard; the pilot gives way
Switch off the main battery isolator
Press Auto again to cancel the course
why: Standby releases the autopilot drive so the wheel answers you.

q: At check-in the base points out the emergency tiller in the lazarette. What do you do?
a: Try it on the rudder stock and stow it handy
o: Leave it there — it is for the surveyor
Put it ashore — the wheel has a spare cable
Nothing — the autopilot steers if needed
why: The emergency tiller is useless if nobody knows where it fits or where it lives.

q: Raising the anchor, the windlass stops and its breaker has tripped. What do you do?
a: Let it cool, find the cause, reset it once
o: Hold the breaker on and keep winding
Fit a bigger breaker from the spares
Switch off the engine and try again
why: The breaker protects the motor and wiring; something is overloading it.

q: You are about to raise the anchor with the electric windlass. What do you do first?
a: Start the engine to support the battery
o: Stop the engine to save the battery
Turn the battery isolator off
Switch on the bow thruster too
why: A windlass draws over 100 A; the running alternator keeps the voltage up.

q: The chain has jumped off the gypsy. A crew member reaches in to free it while another stands on the foot switch. What do you say?
a: Switch the windlass off at the breaker
o: Keep winding slowly while he frees it
Let him wear gloves and carry on
Use the up switch in short bursts only
why: A windlass can take a finger in an instant; switch it off at the breaker before hands go near the gypsy.

q: The boat has rested all afternoon with nothing switched on. What does the house bank reading tell you?
a: About half charged — time to charge
o: About 90 % — no need to charge
About 10 % — the bank is ruined
Fully charged — 12 V is the target
why: Resting 12.7 V ≈ full, 12.2 V ≈ 50 %, below 12.0 V deeply discharged.

q: The engine is running. A crew member says the batteries are being overcharged. Are they right?
a: No — it is normal while charging
o: Yes — stop the engine at once
Yes — turn the isolator off now
Yes — 12.7 V is the safe maximum
why: While charging a 12 V bank reads 13.8–14.4 V.

q: At anchor, how many amp-hours does the house bank supply in a day?
a: About 120 Ah
o: About 12 Ah
About 96 Ah
About 240 Ah
why: Amps × hours for each: 96 + 10 + 10 + 5 = 121 Ah.

q: Starting full, how many days can you stay at anchor before you must charge?
a: 2 days
o: 4 days
1 day
3 days
why: Half of 400 Ah = 200 Ah usable; 200 ÷ 100 = 2 days.

lines: Daily use per 24 h, no solar

q: The house bank is 100 Ah down. Roughly how long must you run the engine to put it back?
a: At least 2½ hours, more as it tapers
o: About 40 minutes at cruising revs
About 10 minutes at high revs
About 1 hour if you rev it up
why: 100 Ah ÷ 40 A = 2.5 h, and the current falls as the bank fills.

lines: Alternator current into the house bank

q: It is a sunny midday at anchor. Why is the solar giving so little?
a: The boom shades part of the panel
o: The controller stops above 50 %
Med heat stops panels working
Solar only charges the engine bank
why: Even a small shadow across one cell cuts a panel's output sharply.

lines: 200 W panel on the stern arch
Boom swinging across it at anchor

q: You arrive at a marina in Croatia and connect shore power. In what order?
a: Boat end first, then the pedestal
o: Pedestal end first, then the boat
Either order with the RCD on
Pedestal first, boat breakers on
why: The live end goes in last and comes out first, so you never handle a live plug.

q: On shore power, the RCD trips every time you switch on the water heater. What do you do?
a: Leave the heater off — it leaks to earth
o: Hold the RCD in until the heater warms
Bypass the RCD for the heater circuit
Run a second shore cable for the heater
why: An RCD trips on current leaking to earth, a shock risk; find the fault, never bypass it.

fig.title: Shore power
lines: RCD trips when heater switched on

q: The base tells you this at the end of the week. What is the most likely cause?
a: Galvanic current through the shore earth
o: Normal wear in warm Med water
Stray current from the bow thruster
The batteries overcharging the hull
why: The shore earth links your underwater metals to other boats; a galvanic isolator blocks that current.

fig.title: Anodes
lines: Week on shore power in a busy marina
Shaft anode half gone in one week

q: At anchor a crew member wants to use a 2000 W hair dryer. Can they?
a: No — it overloads the inverter
o: Yes — once the bank shows 12.7 V
Yes — with the engine idling
Yes — in bursts under a minute
why: An inverter cannot supply more than its rating; it trips or fails.

q: Roughly what current does this draw from the 12 V house bank?
a: About 90 A
o: About 4 A
About 9 A
About 900 A
why: 1000 W ÷ 12 V ≈ 83 A, plus inverter losses.

q: Before a night passage the navigation lights do not work. You reset the breaker and it trips again at once. What do you do?
a: Leave it off and look for a short
o: Hold the breaker on until it stays
Fit a higher-rated breaker
Switch to the other battery bank
why: A breaker that trips straight away is protecting the wiring from a short; find it first.

q: The fridge fuse has blown. Which do you fit from the spares box?
a: The 10 A fuse
o: The 20 A fuse
The 5 A fuse
A strip of foil
why: Replace like with like; a bigger fuse lets the wiring overheat.

q: Anchored overnight with the fridge on, where do you set the battery selector?
a: House bank only
o: Both banks together
Engine bank only
Off for the night
why: Keep the engine battery out of the house loads so you can always start in the morning.

q: This is the house bank first thing in the morning. What do you do?
a: Cut loads and charge now
o: Nothing — a normal reading
Run the fridge off the engine bank
Top up the cells with seawater
why: Below 12.0 V the bank is deeply discharged and damaged if left there.

q: Motoring for two hours, you smell rotten eggs near the battery locker. What is happening?
a: Overcharging — stop charging, ventilate
o: Normal fast charge — open the locker
Holding tank smell — pump out soon
Diesel leak — check the fuel filter
why: Above about 14.8 V a faulty regulator boils the batteries and they give off gas.

lines: Battery cases warm to the touch

q: The water pump keeps running but the tap only spits air. What do you do?
a: Switch off the pump and change tanks
o: Leave the pump on to clear the air
Fit a bigger fuse to the pump
Prime it with the galley tap open
why: The tank is empty; a pump running dry burns out.

fig.title: Galley tap
lines: Air and spluttering from the tap

q: At night, with every tap closed, you hear the water pump run for a few seconds every few minutes. Why?
a: A leak or a dripping tap somewhere
o: Normal — it keeps the pressure up
The tanks are full and overflowing
The water heater is warming up
why: A pressure pump only runs when water leaves the system; look in the bilge too.

fig.title: Water pump
lines: All taps closed, no one using water

q: How many days can you go before refilling the tanks?
a: 3 days
o: 6 days
2 days
5 days

fig.title: Water
lines: Careful use: 20 litres each a day

q: Two days from the next water quay, the tanks are a quarter full. Which habit saves the most?
a: Washing up in seawater first
o: Switching off the water heater
Drinking bottled water instead
Pumping the heads less often
why: Washing up and showers use the most fresh water; the heads already flush with seawater.

q: Your charter boat has a watermaker. Where do you avoid running it?
a: In the marina, where oily water fouls it
o: Offshore, where the water is saltier
At anchor over clean sand
Under sail, while the boat heels
why: Oil and dirt in harbour water ruin the membrane; make water in clean sea.

q: At anchor with no shore power, the crew want hot showers. When will the water be hot?
a: After motoring — the engine heats it
o: Any time — the heater runs off the batteries
Only after the gas boiler is lit
Only once the solar has charged
why: The calorifier is heated by engine coolant, or by its 230 V element on shore power.

q: You arrive in a Croatian marina for the night. Where do you set the heads Y-valve?
a: Holding tank — nothing overboard
o: Overboard, with plenty of flushing
Overboard — the marina is flushed
Either — rules apply at anchor only
why: No sewage goes overboard in marinas and harbours; use the holding tank and a pump-out.

q: Your holding tank is full and you are anchored in a small crowded bay. What do you do?
a: Empty it at a pump-out or far offshore
o: Empty it now — the tide carries it away
Empty it at night when nobody swims
Empty it here if you add a cleaner
why: Only discharge at a pump-out station or well out to sea where local rules allow.

q: In Göcek a Turkish coastguard officer asks to see your blue card. What is it?
a: A log of your holding-tank pump-outs
o: Your VHF radio operator's licence
Proof of the boat's third-party cover
Your cruising permit for Turkey
why: Turkey's blue card logs each pump-out; boats without a record risk a heavy fine.

q: Sailing heeled, you find the heads bowl slowly filling with seawater. What is happening?
a: Seawater siphons in through the inlet
o: The holding tank is overflowing back
Rain from the deck is draining in
The bilge pump is pushing water back
why: Heeled, the inlet can siphon if its seacock is open; close heads seacocks after use.

fig.title: Heads
lines: Bowl slowly filling with clean seawater
Y-valve set to the holding tank

q: You check the engine-intake seacock. Is it open or closed?
a: Closed
o: Open
Half open
It depends on the maker
why: A ball-valve seacock is open when the handle lies along the pipe, closed when across it.

q: At check-in, the galley sink seacock will not turn. What do you do?
a: Report it to the base before you sail
o: Leave it — seacocks are meant to stay fixed
Hammer the handle until it moves
Grease the handle and sail anyway
why: Every seacock must close in an emergency; exercise them and get a seized one fixed.

q: This is what you find under the aft cabin. What do you do first?
a: Hammer in the softwood bung
o: Close the seacock above the break
Run the bilge pump and wait
Stuff a towel in and keep sailing
why: A tapered softwood bung, tied beside each through-hull, plugs a broken fitting.

fig.title: Leak
lines: Through-hull snapped off below its seacock
Water pouring in through the hole
Tapered wooden bung tied beside it

q: Sailing on a beam reach, the electric bilge pump runs every ten minutes. What do you do?
a: Find the source — start by tasting it
o: Nothing — pumps cycle when boats heel
Switch the pump off to save the battery
Close all seacocks and keep sailing
why: Fresh means a tank or pipe; salt means a through-hull, stern gland or rudder seal.

q: The bilge is full, but the manual pump moves almost no water. What do you check first?
a: The strum box at the end of the hose
o: The cockpit drain seacock
The electric pump's float switch
The pump handle's locking pin
why: The strum box keeps debris out of the pump; when it clogs, the pump sucks nothing.

fig.title: Manual bilge pump
lines: Bilge water over the floor boards
Handle pumps easily, little water out

q: At the berth, the electric bilge pump runs non-stop, but the bilge is dry. What is wrong?
a: The float switch is stuck up
o: The pump is blocked by debris
Normal — it keeps the bilge dry
The hull is leaking into the keel
why: A jammed float switch runs the pump dry until it burns out or flattens the battery.

q: You light the cooker but no gas comes through. What do you do?
a: Switch on the gas solenoid
o: Change the bottle for a new one
Open the burner knob wider
Bleed the gas line at the cooker
why: The solenoid valve at the bottle shuts the gas off until switched on at its panel.

q: You have finished cooking. How do you turn the gas off?
a: Solenoid off first, then the burner knob
o: Burner knob off, then the solenoid
Burner knob only; leave the solenoid on
Bottle valve only; leave the knob open
why: Shutting the supply first burns off the gas left in the pipe.

q: At check-in you find the gas locker's drain hole blocked with rubbish. Why does it matter?
a: Leaked gas cannot drain overboard
o: Rainwater will rust the bottle
The solenoid cannot vent heat
The regulator will freeze up
why: Bottled gas is heavier than air; the locker drain lets any leak run out over the side.

q: You are filling the tender's outboard. Which do you use?
a: Plain unleaded petrol
o: Petrol mixed with 2T oil
Diesel from the yacht
Any of the three
why: A four-stroke has its own oil sump; only two-strokes take oil mixed in the fuel.

q: You have just started the tender's outboard alongside the yacht. What do you do?
a: Stop it — no cooling water flowing
o: Normal — it only flows at full throttle
Normal — the jet is for the exhaust
Carry on and check it at the beach
why: The tell-tale stream shows the water pump is working; without it the engine overheats.

lines: No water from the tell-tale hole

q: On the beach, the outboard refuses to start. What is the fix?
a: Clip on the kill cord
o: Take out the spark plug
Pull with more choke
Tip the engine up
why: With the kill cord off, the stop switch keeps the engine from running.

fig.title: Outboard
lines: Fuel tap open, tank half full
Choke out, ten pulls, no firing

q: Heading back from the beach, the outboard does this. What is the likely cause?
a: The fuel tank vent is closed
o: The spark plug is fouled
The kill cord is too long
The fuel mix is too rich
why: A closed vent builds a vacuum in the tank until fuel stops; a pause lets air in again.

fig.title: Outboard
lines: Restarts after a rest, then dies again
Fuel in the tank, choke off

q: First start of the day, the outboard is cold. How do you use the choke?
a: Pull it out, push it in as it warms
o: Leave it in — choke is for hot engines
Pull it out and leave it all day
Use it only after the engine stalls
why: Choke richens the mixture for a cold start; left out, it floods and stalls the engine.

q: At the fuel berth, how do you stop diesel spraying out of the tank breather?
a: Fill slowly and hold a rag at the vent
o: Fill fast so the nozzle cuts out
Fill to the brim so no air is left
Tape over the breather before filling
why: The breather lets air out; when fuel comes up it, the tank is full. Spills are fined.
